target.title: Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood
target.thesis: God satisfies divine simplicity by being a part of all his parts, so the doctrine is best formulated as a symmetry-of-parthood thesis about God's relation to his attributes, which avoids the distinctness and modal collapse objections.

W7212186029.a1.quote: the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation.

W7212186029.a2.text: Common objections to divine simplicity concern distinctness of God’s attributes and modal‑collapse arguments.
W7212186029.a2.quote: The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

W7212186029.a3.text: The symmetry formulation is viable because parthood can model instantiation and it preserves motivations from aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.

Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.

W7212186029.c001.text: The doctrine of divine simplicity says that God lacks proper parts, but it is also often formulated as identifying God with all his parts.
W7212186029.c001.quote: Taken at face value, the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) says that God lacks proper parts, but the doctrine is also often formulated as a thesis identifying God with all his parts.

W7212186029.c002.text: The two formulations are not generally equivalent because, on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts.
W7212186029.c002.quote: The two formulations are not generally equivalent – on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its (possibly distinct) parts.

W7212186029.c003.text: Therefore the doctrine of divine simplicity can be alternatively formulated as the thesis that God is part of all his parts, called the symmetry formulation.
W7212186029.c003.quote: Thus, the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation.

W7212186029.c004.text: The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes because instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood.
W7212186029.c004.quote: The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes, because instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood.

W7212186029.c005.text: The symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity derived from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.
W7212186029.c005.quote: Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.

W7212186029.c006.text: The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity concerning distinctness in God’s attributes and modal collapse arguments.
W7212186029.c006.quote: The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

W7212186029.c007.text: Under classical mereology, the two formulations of the doctrine of divine simplicity are equivalent: something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.
W7212186029.c007.quote: Under classical mereology, the two formulations of DDS are equivalent – something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.

W7212186029.c008.text: If proper parthood is defined as non‑symmetric parthood, then the mereological formulation yields the symmetry formulation of the doctrine of divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c008.quote: If proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood, then explicating proper parthood in the mereological formulation yields the symmetry formulation of DDS.

W7212186029.c009.text: When antisymmetry is not assumed, the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is strictly weaker than the identity formulation: lacking distinct parts entails lacking non‑symmetric parts, but not the reverse.
W7212186029.c009.quote: Accordingly, DDS under the symmetric formulation is strictly weaker than under the identity formulation: if God lacks distinct parts, he also lacks non-symmetric parts, but not vice versa.

W7212186029.c010.text: Thus, within the formal mereological framework, the symmetry formulation provides a viable and distinct way of understanding the doctrine of divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c010.quote: The upshot is that as far as the formal mereological framework goes, the symmetry formulation presents a viable and distinct way of understanding DDS.

W7212186029.c011.text: Adopting the symmetry formulation does not require abandoning the identity formulation nor discarding antisymmetry from the concept of parthood.
W7212186029.c011.quote: Tobesure,adoptingthesymmetryformulationdoesnotrequireabandoningtheidentityformulationaltogether, nor is it being suggested that antisymmetry should be altogether dropped from our concept of parthood.

W7212186029.c012.text: Parthood could follow classical mereology in ordinary cases, with violations of antisymmetry limited to atypical cases such as constitution or instances involving God.
W7212186029.c012.quote: In particular, parthood could obey classical mereology in ordinary instances, with violations of antisymmetry limited to atypical cases like constitution or cases involving God.

W7212186029.c013.text: Some usual motivations for divine simplicity can be upheld by allowing the mereological relations involving God to differ from those between ordinary objects, especially regarding antisymmetry.
W7212186029.c013.quote: Indeed, it will be seen in section ‘Motivations’ that some of the usual motivations for DDS can be upheld by taking the mereological relations involving God to differ from those between ordinary objects, particularly with respect to antisymmetry.

W7212186029.c014.text: The identity formulation of divine simplicity is not excluded by the symmetry formulation and is actually equivalent to it.
W7212186029.c014.quote: the identity formulation of DDS is not ruled out by the symmetry formulation, and is in fact equivalent to it.

W7212186029.c015.text: The symmetry formulation is not meant to be an interpretation of divine simple doctrine as traditionally presented.
W7212186029.c015.quote: the symmetry formulation is not intended to be an interpretation of DDS as traditionally presented.

W7212186029.c016.text: Divine simple doctrine is sometimes understood as the claim that God has no proper parts of any kind.
W7212186029.c016.quote: DDS is sometimes taken to be a general claim that God lacks proper parts of any kind, with some authors even denying that God instantiates composition by being part of something else (Aquinas 2005b).

W7212186029.c017.text: Simplicity concerning God’s attributes distinguishes God more sharply from other entities than simplicity concerning other kinds of parthood, supporting a common motivation from God’s transcendence.
W7212186029.c017.quote: One reason for this focus is that simplicity with respect to attributes would set God apart from other entities more distinctly than simplicity with respect to other kinds of parthood, in line with a common motivation for DDS from God’s transcendence.

W7212186029.c021.quote: the symmetry formulation raises the question of how the relation between objects and their properties can be modelled as a form of parthood.

W7212186029.c022.quote: if the symmetry formulation is to present a genuine alternative to the identity formulation, it should also be plausible that parthood in this sense can violate antisymmetry.

W7212186029.c023.quote: And, it has to be plausible that proper parthood can be defined as non‑symmetric parthood, if the symmetry formulation is to be viable here.

W7212186029.c024.quote: On the mereological bundle theory suggested by Laurie Paul (2002, 2006, 2012, 2017), objects are mereological fusions of the properties they bear.

W7212186029.c025.text: If such cases exist, parthood based on similarity is not generally antisymmetric.
W7212186029.c025.quote: The possibility of such cases would imply that parthood with respect to similarity is not generally antisymmetric.

W7212186029.c026.quote: If proper parthood is defined as non‑symmetric parthood with respect to similarity, it would immediately be irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.

W7212186029.c027.quote: The upshot is that the relations between objects and their properties can be modelled mereologically in such a way that DDS on the symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about the relation between God and his attributes.

W7212186029.c030.quote: if instantiation is modelled as parthood, then for any object at all to have necessary properties requires that some parthood relations be necessary.

W7212186029.c033.quote: Hence, under the symmetry formulation of DDS, God’s nature can be said to admit no discernible divisions, even if his attributes are not numerically identical to each other.

W7212186029.c038.quote: The symmetry formulation offers a possible way in which God’s relation to his attributes can be contingent under DDS, namely, by taking God to be related to some of his attributes by contingent (mutual) parthood relations.

W7212186029.c040.quote: Then, there is a possible world in which God exists (by necessity), but does not have a willingness to create and hence does not, which implies that God’s actual creative act is free.

W7212186029.c045.quote: The parthood relations between God and his omniscience can be taken to be necessary (since omniscience is in God’s intrinsic nature).

W7212186029.c047.quote: That snow is white is thus a contingent truth in actuality.

W7212186029.c048.text: Divine simplicity (DDS) is usually taken to identify God with all his parts, but an alternative thesis is that God is a part of all his parts.
W7212186029.c048.quote: DDS has often been understood as a thesis identifying God with all his parts. However, this paper has argued that there is a viable alternative formulation of DDS as a thesis that God is part of all his parts.

W7212186029.c049.quote: The viability of this formulation is suggested by the observations that there are plausible mereological theories under which mereological simplicity consists in lacking non-symmetric parts.

objections.text: Take a case where instantiation is modeled as parthood and see what breaks. Let a red sphere s instantiate redness r and roundness o. Model instantiation as parthood: r and o are parts of s. Now consider a bare particular b that instantiates nothing. Under the model, b has no parts. Consider a second sphere t that is red and round, and let s and t share both properties. Parthood as a relation among concrete things is transitive and, in standard mereologies, supports fusion: the fusion of r and o would be a part of s, and so would any fusion of attributes. But instantiation is not closed under fusion: a fusion of redness and roundness does not instantiate 'being red-and-round' as a single attribute that s bears in the same way. Worse, if s is a part of its own attribute-fusion, the model forces s to have itself as a proper part in a loop whenever an attribute is predicated of the attribute's bearer, violating the asymmetry that the symmetry formulation was meant to preserve. The modeling therefore cannot be both transitive and asymmetric, so the viability premise's antecedent fails in exactly the mereological framework the conclusion relies on.
objections.premise_fails_because: Instantiation is not plausibly modeled as parthood, since treating it as a transitive, fusion-closed relation generates loops of parthood (a bearer part of its own attribute fusion) that contradict the non-symmetric parthood the symmetry formulation needs.

objections.text: If God instantiates an attribute such as wisdom, modeling that instantiation as parthood makes wisdom a part of God, not God a part of wisdom. The symmetry formulation requires that God be a part of every part of God: whenever something is a part of God, God is also a part of it. The premise assumes that merely modeling instantiation as parthood yields this mutual parthood, but it only establishes a one-directional relation from attribute to substance. Without a further premise ensuring that God is likewise a part of each attribute, the symmetry formulation cannot get off the ground as a thesis about God's relation to his attributes.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7212186029.c004 fails because modeling instantiation as parthood yields only one direction of parthood (attributes as parts of God), whereas the symmetry formulation requires mutual parthood between God and his attributes.

objections.text: Suppose instantiation is parthood. A red apple instantiates redness, so redness is a part of the apple. Redness itself instantiates the property of being a color, so being-a-color is a part of redness. Parthood is transitive: if being-a-color is part of redness and redness is part of the apple, then being-a-color is part of the apple. So the apple instantiates being-a-color, meaning the apple is a color. But the apple is not a color; it is a physical object. Instantiation is not transitive—a thing can instantiate a property which itself instantiates a higher-order property without the thing instantiating that higher-order property—while parthood is. This structural mismatch breaks the modeling at a basic level.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because instantiation lacks the transitivity that parthood has, so modeling instantiation as parthood generates absurd consequences like a red apple being a color.

objections.text: In the practice of crafting a single, seamless vessel from clay, the potter treats the clay as both whole and without separate parts, yet does not claim the clay is identical to all its parts. The clay is unified in form, but its parts (if any) are not conflated with the whole. Here, lack of proper parts does not require identity with those parts, as the vessel’s unity is preserved without collapsing distinctions. The assumption that the two formulations are interchangeable ignores this practical separation between unity and identity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c001 fails because unity does not necessitate identity with parts, as shown in the craft analogy.

objections.text: c004 claims the symmetry formulation is viable because instantiation can be modeled as parthood. This smuggles in the assumption that the relation between God and his attributes is a parthood relation. But the argument needs this assumption and cannot sustain it. If God's being omnipotent is modeled as omnipotence being a part of God, then God has parts—precisely what c001's divine simplicity denies. The symmetry formulation (c008) tries to rescue this by redefining proper parthood as non-symmetric parthood, so that symmetric relations aren't 'proper' parts. But this only works if the underlying relation is already parthood; symmetry is a property of a parthood relation, not a substitute for it. If instantiation is instead a property-possession or grounding relation, there is no parthood to be symmetric about, and the symmetry formulation has no content. c004 cannot have both: it needs instantiation to be parthood to generate the symmetry thesis, yet if it is parthood, God has parts, and the whole project of preserving divine simplicity collapses.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because it requires instantiation to be parthood in order to generate the symmetry formulation, but if instantiation genuinely is parthood, God has parts, directly contradicting the divine simplicity it is meant to preserve.

objections.text: Consider a scenario where God's attributes, such as wisdom and compassion, are distinct yet inseparable aspects of God's nature. In this case, instantiation, or the relationship between God and his attributes, cannot be reduced to a mereological concept like parthood, as it implies a false dichotomy between God's attributes and his essence. For instance, God's wisdom is not a 'part' of God in the classical sense, but rather an intrinsic aspect of God's being. This nuance highlights the limitations of modeling instantiation as parthood.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it oversimplifies the complex relationship between God and his attributes, which cannot be accurately captured by a mereological framework.

objections.text: A community of believers holds that God's wisdom, power, and love are parts of God, and they argue that this is viable because instantiation is modelled as parthood. In truthmaker theory each true statement must be grounded by a concrete reality that makes it true. The statement "God's wisdom is a part of God" would need a truthmaker: an entity that is both God and the particular instantiation of wisdom. Since God's attributes are not distinct entities but modes of a simple being, there is no separate grounding fact that can serve as a truthmaker for the parthood claim. Thus the purported parthood relation is truthmaker‑orphaned, showing the premise that such modelling makes the symmetry formulation viable is false.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c004 fails because the claimed parthood relation lacks a truthmaker, violating truthmaker theory.

objections.text: Consider a bright red rose. If instantiation is modeled as parthood, then redness must be a part of the rose. This implies the rose is a composite entity formed by the mereological sum of a concrete object and an abstract universal. For a Platonist, redness exists as an independent, non-spatial entity that the rose instantiates. A property is not a constituent part that adds to the mereological composition of a particular; it is an entity to which the particular relates. To treat instantiation as parthood incorrectly treats the universal as a constituent component of the particular, destroying the ontological distinction between the realm of universals and the realm of particulars.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because instantiation is a relation between a particular and an independent universal, whereas parthood is a relation between constituents of a single entity.

objections.text: Consider a fire that instantiates heat. On a mereological model of instantiation, heat is an aspectual part of the fire: it cannot exist apart from it and is a constituent of its state. Yet the fire is not part of the heat; the heat is an effect and dependent feature that does not encompass its source. rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection attacks premise c004 as stated. The premise claims the symmetry formulation is viable because instantiation can be modeled as parthood. The objection argues that this modeling only yields one-directional parthood (attribute is part of God), whereas the symmetry formulation requires mutual parthood (God is also part of each attribute). This directly challenges whether the premise's stated reason is sufficient to support its conclusion, which is an attack on the premise as stated, not a misreading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that modeling instantiation as parthood, taken alone, gives a relation running from attribute to God, and that the symmetry formulation needs God to be part of each attribute. But the argument's own structure answers this. The paper's c028 states the symmetry formulation holds that God is part of all his attributes, and c045 and c038 assign God a necessary parthood relation to omniscience, with some attributes standing in contingent mutual parthood to God. So the mutual direction is asserted in the paper's commitments, not inferred from instantiation alone. The gap you identify is real for c004 read in isolation: the inference from 'instantiation can be modeled as parthood' to 'the symmetry formulation is viable' needs the premise that the modeled relation is symmetric in the relevant cases. I would state that as the missing bridge: instantiation, modeled as parthood, must hold in both directions between God and each attribute. Whether that is plausible is exactly what c028 and c045 are there to defend, and I cannot cite independent literature here showing it. So the argument survives only if the bridge is accepted as part of c004's grounding, and I should not pretend the inference from c004 alone is complete.

Revised premise: Instantiation, modeled as parthood, holds symmetrically between God and each of his attributes, so that God is part of each attribute as well as each attribute part of God.

The author can meet this by noting that divine attributes are parts of God's intrinsic nature [W7212186029.c045], which makes mutual parthood plausible here. So the argument survives once we add the premise that the divine parthood relation is symmetric.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W7212186029.c004's claim that 'instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood' by arguing that, under such a modeling, parthood's transitivity and fusion properties generate problems that instantiation lacks, and that the model introduces proper-part loops. The objection does not misread the argument into a different premise or conclusion; it targets exactly the modeling claim the premise relies on.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The objection says the modeling cannot be both transitive and asymmetric, but the argument never claims that instantiation is closed under fusion or that every attribute-fusion is a part of its bearer. The viability claim needs only that some parthood-style relation between God and his attributes is non-symmetric, so that proper parthood is well defined, and transitive, as c026 specifies [W7212186029.c026]. The loop worry depends on predication being modeled as a relation from the attribute back to its bearer, which the argument does not require: the symmetry formulation concerns God's relation to his attributes, not the attributes' relation to God. The bare particular b is irrelevant, since the thesis concerns only God, who instantiates his attributes and so is not a bare particular. On the constituent ontology, properties are parts of their bearers [W2571599220.a1; W2594652691.a1], which is the direction the model uses, and asymmetry holds because the attributes are not parts of each other in a cycle. The fusion worry is real for a general theory of instantiation, and I grant that instantiation is not closed under fusion, but the argument does not need that closure. Where the objection bites is the necessity worry raised by c030: if instantiation is parthood, necessary properties force necessary parthood facts [W7212186029.c030]. That is a further commitment the argument should flag rather than hide. I concede that c004 is stated more strongly than the modeling supports, and I would weaken it to the claim that, for God and his attributes, instantiation can be modeled as non-symmetric parthood, without commitment to fusion closure.
rounds.revised_premise: For God and his attributes, instantiation can be modeled as a non-symmetric, transitive parthood relation, without any commitment that instantiation is closed under mereological fusion.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You concede that c004 is stated too strongly, and you propose the weaker claim that God's relation to his attributes can be modeled as non-symmetric parthood. That weaker claim still defeats the viability premise, and your reply does not address why.

The symmetry formulation says God lacks non-symmetric parts. Your model says that instantiation is parthood, and on your reply's own constituent ontology, properties are parts of their bearers. So God's attributes are non-symmetric parts of God. If the model applies to God, the thesis you are trying to make viable is denied, not modeled.

You could block this by making the parthood relation hold only in the direction attribute-to-God, so that God is not the whole of which the attributes are parts. But then the relation is not parthood in the sense the framework needs, and the mereological definition of proper parthood no longer applies to God. Either way, the viability claim requires a model in which God has no non-symmetric parts while his attributes stand in a parthood relation to him. Your reply supplies no such model, so c004 does not hold even in its weakened form.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my weakened c004 fails as I stated it. If the constituent ontology makes attributes parts of their bearers [W2571599220.a1; W2594652691.a1], then in the one-directional model God has his attributes as non-symmetric parts, which is exactly what the symmetry formulation denies. My claim that asymmetry holds because attributes are not parts of each other in a cycle was muddled, and I withdraw it. The objector's dilemma omits a third option. The symmetry formulation needs God and each attribute to be parts of one another, so that neither is a proper part. Mutual parthood is what the framework already supplies: parts of each other share all their parts and are parts of all the same things [W7212186029.c032]. Under that model, God lacks non-symmetric parts while his attributes stand in a parthood relation to him. That is a model with no non-symmetric parts for God, which answers your demand. The cost is that mutual parthood collapses the difference between God and his attributes at the level of parts, and the necessity worry from [W7212186029.c030] still applies. I accept that cost as a further commitment to flag, not a refutation. So the premise must change: instantiation between God and his attributes is modeled as symmetric parthood, which makes the attributes improper parts.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that r1, read as a claim that instantiation holds symmetrically between God and each attribute, is hard to defend by analogy with the fire and heat. The heat is a dependent feature, and the fire is not part of it in any ordinary sense. But the argument does not need the fire analogy to carry the symmetry. The viability premise [W7212186029.c004] says only that instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood, and the revision r2 adopted after your kind of trial makes the symmetry a feature of the model itself, namely that for God and his attributes instantiation is modeled as mutual parthood. Your schema is a different model, one in which instantiation is asymmetric, and nothing in the argument says that model is the one to use for God. Your point does show that the symmetric model is a choice, not a discovery, and that the intuitive case for it is weak. That matters for whether the symmetry formulation is the most natural reading of simplicity, which the conclusion [W7212186029.c010] does not claim. The conclusion claims only viability and distinctness. Divine concurrence [W1563585053.a1] and the formal-cause reading [W7162684616.a2], which make God a metaphysical part of creatures, are asymmetric pictures that you might press, but they concern God's relation to creatures rather than to his attributes, so they do not settle the matter either way. I concede that r1 as stated does not survive, and the argument should rest on r2 alone.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede the symmetry is a stipulated choice lacking intuitive support. But viability is not mere formal consistency. If we model God’s relation to his attributes as mutual parthood, we need some metaphysical reason to think God is actually part of his goodness or power, not just a formal postulate tailored to block proper parthood. Without that, r2 is a formal artifact, not a model of instantiation. A thesis about divine simplicity is viable only if it illuminates the underlying metaphysics. You have given no account of why the God-attribute relation is symmetric rather than an asymmetric dependence like substance and property. Until you do, the symmetry formulation is an unmotivated formalism, and its alleged viability is unsupported.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the symmetry is a modeling choice, and I will not pretend the fire-and-heat intuition favours mutual parthood. But your rejoinder asks for more than the conclusion needs. The conclusion [W7212186029.c010] claims only that the symmetry formulation is viable and distinct within the formal framework, and viability in that sense is shown by a consistent model in which God lacks non-symmetric parts while being part of each attribute. That model is available and coherent, so the formal demand is met. Your further demand, that the model illuminate the metaphysics, is a demand for motivation, and I accept that the current text supplies little. The best available motivation is that the symmetric model, unlike the asymmetric one, does not treat God's attributes as dependent proper parts, which fits the simplicity intuition that nothing in God is a proper constituent [W4235072123.a1]. Whether that motivation is adequate is open. I also note that the asymmetric pictures I cited, such as the formal-cause reading [W7162684616.a2] and grounding rather than causal dependence [W4229080938.c030], concern creatures or grounding and do not directly decide the God-attribute case. My final position: the argument survives only as a claim of formal viability, not as a claim that the symmetric model is metaphysically preferred. Since the conclusion does not rest on that preference, the argument as stated survives in weakened form, provided the conclusion is read narrowly.

objection.text: Take a case where instantiation is modeled as parthood and see what breaks. Let a red sphere s instantiate redness r and roundness o. Model instantiation as parthood: r and o are parts of s. Now consider a bare particular b that instantiates nothing. Under the model, b has no parts. Consider a second sphere t that is red and round, and let s and t share both properties. Parthood as a relation among concrete things is transitive and, in standard mereologies, supports fusion: the fusion of r and o would be a part of s, and so would any fusion of attributes. But instantiation is not closed under fusion: a fusion of redness and roundness does not instantiate 'being red-and-round' as a single attribute that s bears in the same way. Worse, if s is a part of its own attribute-fusion, the model forces s to have itself as a proper part in a loop whenever an attribute is predicated of the attribute's bearer, violating the asymmetry that the symmetry formulation was meant to preserve. The modeling therefore cannot be both transitive and asymmetric, so the viability premise's antecedent fails in exactly the mereological framework the conclusion relies on.
objection.premise_fails_because: Instantiation is not plausibly modeled as parthood, since treating it as a transitive, fusion-closed relation generates loops of parthood (a bearer part of its own attribute fusion) that contradict the non-symmetric parthood the symmetry formulation needs.

objection.text: If God instantiates an attribute such as wisdom, modeling that instantiation as parthood makes wisdom a part of God, not God a part of wisdom. The symmetry formulation requires that God be a part of every part of God: whenever something is a part of God, God is also a part of it. The premise assumes that merely modeling instantiation as parthood yields this mutual parthood, but it only establishes a one-directional relation from attribute to substance. Without a further premise ensuring that God is likewise a part of each attribute, the symmetry formulation cannot get off the ground as a thesis about God's relation to his attributes.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W7212186029.c004 fails because modeling instantiation as parthood yields only one direction of parthood (attributes as parts of God), whereas the symmetry formulation requires mutual parthood between God and his attributes.

objection.text: Suppose instantiation is parthood. A red apple instantiates redness, so redness is a part of the apple. Redness itself instantiates the property of being a color, so being-a-color is a part of redness. Parthood is transitive: if being-a-color is part of redness and redness is part of the apple, then being-a-color is part of the apple. So the apple instantiates being-a-color, meaning the apple is a color. But the apple is not a color; it is a physical object. Instantiation is not transitive—a thing can instantiate a property which itself instantiates a higher-order property without the thing instantiating that higher-order property—while parthood is. This structural mismatch breaks the modeling at a basic level.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because instantiation lacks the transitivity that parthood has, so modeling instantiation as parthood generates absurd consequences like a red apple being a color.

objection.text: In the practice of crafting a single, seamless vessel from clay, the potter treats the clay as both whole and without separate parts, yet does not claim the clay is identical to all its parts. The clay is unified in form, but its parts (if any) are not conflated with the whole. Here, lack of proper parts does not require identity with those parts, as the vessel’s unity is preserved without collapsing distinctions. The assumption that the two formulations are interchangeable ignores this practical separation between unity and identity.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c001 fails because unity does not necessitate identity with parts, as shown in the craft analogy.

objection.text: c004 claims the symmetry formulation is viable because instantiation can be modeled as parthood. This smuggles in the assumption that the relation between God and his attributes is a parthood relation. But the argument needs this assumption and cannot sustain it. If God's being omnipotent is modeled as omnipotence being a part of God, then God has parts—precisely what c001's divine simplicity denies. The symmetry formulation (c008) tries to rescue this by redefining proper parthood as non-symmetric parthood, so that symmetric relations aren't 'proper' parts. But this only works if the underlying relation is already parthood; symmetry is a property of a parthood relation, not a substitute for it. If instantiation is instead a property-possession or grounding relation, there is no parthood to be symmetric about, and the symmetry formulation has no content. c004 cannot have both: it needs instantiation to be parthood to generate the symmetry thesis, yet if it is parthood, God has parts, and the whole project of preserving divine simplicity collapses.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because it requires instantiation to be parthood in order to generate the symmetry formulation, but if instantiation genuinely is parthood, God has parts, directly contradicting the divine simplicity it is meant to preserve.

objection.text: Consider a scenario where God's attributes, such as wisdom and compassion, are distinct yet inseparable aspects of God's nature. In this case, instantiation, or the relationship between God and his attributes, cannot be reduced to a mereological concept like parthood, as it implies a false dichotomy between God's attributes and his essence. For instance, God's wisdom is not a 'part' of God in the classical sense, but rather an intrinsic aspect of God's being. This nuance highlights the limitations of modeling instantiation as parthood.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it oversimplifies the complex relationship between God and his attributes, which cannot be accurately captured by a mereological framework.

objection.text: A community of believers holds that God's wisdom, power, and love are parts of God, and they argue that this is viable because instantiation is modelled as parthood. In truthmaker theory each true statement must be grounded by a concrete reality that makes it true. The statement "God's wisdom is a part of God" would need a truthmaker: an entity that is both God and the particular instantiation of wisdom. Since God's attributes are not distinct entities but modes of a simple being, there is no separate grounding fact that can serve as a truthmaker for the parthood claim. Thus the purported parthood relation is truthmaker‑orphaned, showing the premise that such modelling makes the symmetry formulation viable is false.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c004 fails because the claimed parthood relation lacks a truthmaker, violating truthmaker theory.

objection.text: Consider a bright red rose. If instantiation is modeled as parthood, then redness must be a part of the rose. This implies the rose is a composite entity formed by the mereological sum of a concrete object and an abstract universal. For a Platonist, redness exists as an independent, non-spatial entity that the rose instantiates. A property is not a constituent part that adds to the mereological composition of a particular; it is an entity to which the particular relates. To treat instantiation as parthood incorrectly treats the universal as a constituent component of the particular, destroying the ontological distinction between the realm of universals and the realm of particulars.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because instantiation is a relation between a particular and an independent universal, whereas parthood is a relation between constituents of a single entity.

turn.content: Not a misreading: The objection attacks premise c004 as stated. The premise claims the symmetry formulation is viable because instantiation can be modeled as parthood. The objection argues that this modeling only yields one-directional parthood (attribute is part of God), whereas the symmetry formulation requires mutual parthood (God is also part of each attribute). turn.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W7212186029.c004's claim that 'instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood' by arguing that, under such a modeling, parthood's transitivity and fusion properties generate problems that instantiation lacks, and that the model introduces proper-part loops. This is an attack on the premise as stated, however weak or flawed the attack may be. The objection does not misread the argument into a different premise or conclusion; it targets exactly the modeling claim the premise relies on.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that modeling instantiation as parthood, taken alone, gives a relation running from attribute to God, and that the symmetry formulation needs God to be part of each attribute. But the argument's own structure answers this. The paper's c028 states the symmetry formulation holds that God is part of all his attributes, and c045 and c038 assign God a necessary parthood relation to omniscience, with some attributes standing in contingent mutual parthood to God. So the mutual direction is asserted in the paper's commitments, not inferred from instantiation alone. The gap you identify is real for c004 read in isolation: the inference from 'instantiation can be modeled as parthood' to 'the symmetry formulation is viable' needs the premise that the modeled relation is symmetric in the relevant cases. I would state that as the missing bridge: instantiation, modeled as parthood, must hold in both directions between God and each attribute. Whether that is plausible is exactly what c028 and c045 are there to defend, and I cannot cite independent literature here showing it. So the argument survives only if the bridge is accepted as part of c004's grounding, and I should not pretend the inference from c004 alone is complete.

Revised premise: Instantiation, modeled as parthood, holds symmetrically between God and each of his attributes, so that God is part of each attribute as well as each attribute part of God.
turn.revised_premise: Instantiation, modeled as parthood, holds symmetrically between God and each of his attributes, so that God is part of each attribute as well as each attribute part of God.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: The objection says the modeling cannot be both transitive and asymmetric, but the argument never claims that instantiation is closed under fusion or that every attribute-fusion is a part of its bearer. The viability claim needs only that some parthood-style relation between God and his attributes is non-symmetric, so that proper parthood is well defined, and transitive, as c026 specifies [W7212186029.c026]. The loop worry depends on predication being modeled as a relation from the attribute back to its bearer, which the argument does not require: the symmetry formulation concerns God's relation to his attributes, not the attributes' relation to God. The bare particular b is irrelevant, since the thesis concerns only God, who instantiates his attributes and so is not a bare particular. On the constituent ontology, properties are parts of their bearers [W2571599220.a1; W2594652691.a1], which is the direction the model uses, and asymmetry holds because the attributes are not parts of each other in a cycle. The fusion worry is real for a general theory of instantiation, and I grant that instantiation is not closed under fusion, but the argument does not need that closure. Where the objection bites is the necessity worry raised by c030: if instantiation is parthood, necessary properties force necessary parthood facts [W7212186029.c030]. That is a further commitment the argument should flag rather than hide. I concede that c004 is stated more strongly than the modeling supports, and I would weaken it to the claim that, for God and his attributes, instantiation can be modeled as non-symmetric parthood, without commitment to fusion closure.
turn.revised_premise: For God and his attributes, instantiation can be modeled as a non-symmetric, transitive parthood relation, without any commitment that instantiation is closed under mereological fusion.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content:
You concede that c004 is stated too strongly, and you propose the weaker claim that God's relation to his attributes can be modeled as non-symmetric parthood. That weaker claim still defeats the viability premise, and your reply does not address why.

The symmetry formulation says God lacks non-symmetric parts. Your model says that instantiation is parthood, and on your reply's own constituent ontology, properties are parts of their bearers. So God's attributes are non-symmetric parts of God. If the model applies to God, the thesis you are trying to make viable is denied, not modeled.

You could block this by making the parthood relation hold only in the direction attribute-to-God, so that God is not the whole of which the attributes are parts. But then the relation is not parthood in the sense the framework needs, and the mereological definition of proper parthood no longer applies to God. Either way, the viability claim requires a model in which God has no non-symmetric parts while his attributes stand in a parthood relation to him. Your reply supplies no such model, so c004 does not hold even in its weakened form.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that my weakened c004 fails as I stated it. If the constituent ontology makes attributes parts of their bearers [W2571599220.a1; W2594652691.a1], then in the one-directional model God has his attributes as non-symmetric parts, which is exactly what the symmetry formulation denies. My claim that asymmetry holds because attributes are not parts of each other in a cycle was muddled, and I withdraw it. The objector's dilemma omits a third option. The symmetry formulation needs God and each attribute to be parts of one another, so that neither is a proper part. Mutual parthood is what the framework already supplies: parts of each other share all their parts and are parts of all the same things [W7212186029.c032]. Under that model, God lacks non-symmetric parts while his attributes stand in a parthood relation to him. That is a model with no non-symmetric parts for God, which answers your demand. The cost is that mutual parthood collapses the difference between God and his attributes at the level of parts, and the necessity worry from [W7212186029.c030] still applies. I accept that cost as a further commitment to flag, not a refutation. So the premise must change: instantiation between God and his attributes is modeled as symmetric parthood, which makes the attributes improper parts.

Revised premise: For God and his attributes, instantiation is modeled as symmetric (mutual) parthood, so the attributes are not proper parts of God and God lacks non-symmetric parts, without commitment to fusion closure.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You treat 'modeling instantiation as parthood' as importing standard asymmetric parthood, but the argument explicitly drops antisymmetry [W7212186029.c008]. c004 does not claim that modeling instantiation as parthood automatically entails mutual parthood; it claims that because the God-attribute relation can be construed as parthood, the symmetry formulation is conceptually available. The symmetry formulation itself posits that God is part of all his attributes [W7212186029.c028], and the framework allows this without collapse into identity [W7212186029.c009]. Still, you rightly identify a gap: the mere fact that instantiation is parthood does not by itself specify directionality. The author can meet this by noting that divine attributes are parts of God's intrinsic nature [W7212186029.c045], which makes mutual parthood plausible here. So the argument survives once we add the premise that the divine parthood relation is symmetric.

Revised premise: In the divine case, the parthood relation between God and each attribute is symmetric because those attributes are intrinsic parts of God's nature.

You misread the argument's scope: the viability claim is specifically about God's relation to his attributes [W7212186029.c004], not a general theory of ordinary objects. The symmetry formulation is introduced by dropping antisymmetry [W7212186029.c009], so it does not aim to preserve asymmetry; rather, proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood, which remains irreflexive and asymmetric [W7212186029.c026]. Under this definition, mutual parthood between God and an attribute yields no proper-parthood loop. turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content: You concede the symmetry is a stipulated choice lacking intuitive support. But viability is not mere formal consistency. Without that, r2 is a formal artifact, not a model of instantiation. A thesis about divine simplicity is viable only if it illuminates the underlying metaphysics. turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that the symmetry is a modeling choice, and I will not pretend the fire-and-heat intuition favours mutual parthood. But your rejoinder asks for more than the conclusion needs. The conclusion [W7212186029.c010] claims only that the symmetry formulation is viable and distinct within the formal framework, and viability in that sense is shown by a consistent model in which God lacks non-symmetric parts while being part of each attribute. That model is available and coherent, so the formal demand is met. Your further demand, that the model illuminate the metaphysics, is a demand for motivation, and I accept that the current text supplies little. The best available motivation is that the symmetric model, unlike the asymmetric one, does not treat God's attributes as dependent proper parts, which fits the simplicity intuition that nothing in God is a proper constituent [W4235072123.a1]. Whether that motivation is adequate is open. I also note that the asymmetric pictures I cited, such as the formal-cause reading [W7162684616.a2] and grounding rather than causal dependence [W4229080938.c030], concern creatures or grounding and do not directly decide the God-attribute case. My final position: the argument survives only as a claim of formal viability, not as a claim that the symmetric model is metaphysically preferred. Since the conclusion does not rest on that preference, the argument as stated survives in weakened form, provided the conclusion is read narrowly.

turn.content: Misreading: The objection attacks the viability of modeling instantiation as parthood on truthmaker-theoretic grounds, treating the premise as making a metaphysical claim about actual parthood relations requiring truthmakers. However, the argument's revised premise (r3) explicitly states that the model is 'adopted as a formal option rather than as the metaphysically preferred account,' and the conclusion (c010) frames viability 'within the formal mereological framework.' The objection thus attacks a stronger version of the premise than the one stated, importing metaphysical commitments the argument explicitly disclaims.

turn.content: Misreading: The premise claims mutual parthood is consistent with God LACKING non-symmetric parts. The objection argues that mutual parthood 'introduces symmetry,' which it says conflicts with non-symmetry and undermines the argument's distinction. But the premise never claims mutual parthood is non-symmetric or is a proper part; it claims the opposite—that mutual (symmetric) parthood is compatible with the ABSENCE of non-symmetric parts. The objection's own observation that mutual parthood is symmetric actually supports the premise's claim rather than undermining it. The objection attacks the premise as if it asserted compatibility between mutual parthood and HAVING non-symmetric parts, which it does not.
